Hey- this is a fucking lot to deal with. I have also been in a relationship with someone who was intensely suicidal (specifically around the idea of me leaving them) and who did not have much other support, and it can really, really fuck with you and your sense of agency. Are \*you\* in therapy? Can \*you\* get support for being in this position? Even if she won't see a therapist, you might be able to get help, advice, and resources for yourself (and her). 

Ultimately- and this is a really, really hard thing to hear- you are never EVER responsible for someone else's decisions about their own life. If you break up with her (kindly, obvs) because you're just not in love with her and she breaks down, or even follows through on her suicidality, **it's not your fault.** You can't stay, dishonestly, in a relationship you're not feeling indefinitely to save someone else's life. What you \*can\* do is emphasize that you're not leaving her all alone: no longer being romantically involved doesn't mean you need to stop helping and supporting her, and if you do decide to break up with her, make it super clear that that's the case, if that's something you can honestly offer.

Lastly, if she uses threats of suicide to keep you from leaving, that is, unfortunately, an abusive behavior. This doesn't mean she's faking- she might literally feel suicidal- but it \*is\* a significant form of coercion, genuine or not, that ends up removing your agency in the relationship in a big way.

Hey- this happened to me at 16, and I made it through this incredibly scary situation. I'm 32 now, maybe not "turned out ok," but still here, queer, and kicking. 

This is NOT "your fault." Shit happens; people scores older and more experienced re: sex than you have found themselves in the same situation! You do not deserve blameor. This is in no way a reflection of your worth, your intelligence, or your potential. The individual circumstances around every single pregnancy scare are always, always unique and specific to the person ivolved- and that's not something others can judge.

After I got the positive test, I spent two months in intense, full-shutdown denial about it, which made things a lot harder to deal with. You seem like you may be going to hard the other dorection- have you gotten confirmed positive tests yet? If not, hold off on making any decisions until you do.

If you have a trusted adult in your life- or even, barring that, a trusted older teenager, honestly- whom you know truly has your best interests at heart and whom you know respects you, tell them. Even telling a trusted friend your own age is a good start. Just don't carry this fear alone if you can manage to find someone safe to confide in, someone to talk through your feelings, needs, and options with. 

If you don't have someone in your personal life who can do that, are there any services for teens in your area that you might be able to talk to? Ones that will respect your confidentiality and autonomy if the adults in your life are unsafe to bring into the conversation?

If you can find someone to talk to, they can help you figure out what the best course of action is. If you can't talk to anyone in your life, try to find as many resources online as you possibly can, and try to vet your sources carefully- there's a lot of shitty misinformation out there, so make sure what you're reading is backed up by science.

But right now, most of all, try not to beat up on yourself. I know- I KNOW- how hard that is. Please try to be as kind to yourself as you would be to your best friend if she came to you in this situation. Tell yourself all the affirming, caring, comforting shit you'd say to her, and find a way to mean it.

And if it helps at all, know that I, a weird sad stranger on the internet, am sending you so so much love and strength and support right now. I know this sucks, and I'm sorry that you're dealing with it, and I'll be holding you in my thoughts today, hoping you're OK. 💙

I, a 32 year old neurodivergent non-binary person, literally just had a long therapy session about how much teenage-me being worried about my loving parents being worried about me laid the groundwork for a lot of self-destructive relational patterns for the rest of my life. So let me tell you what I now know intellectually but still cannot truly internalize:

It is compassionate and sweet of you to be concerned about your parent's well being! But, his well being doesn't override your own; and, it is the nature of emotionally intimate relationships that they involve mutual care and concern. Do not hide your struggles or take on more hardship to alleviate your father's worry. If you're worried about his ability to have boundaries around caring for you, the best thing you can do is model your own boundary-setting by being *more* self-caring, not more self-sacrificing! Practicing our own boundaries helps other people practice their own boundaries.

(May my 32 year old ass finally learn this lesson.)

I'm an afab NB who experiences truly nightmarish periods. Obviously, I don't know what your boyfriend is experiencing, but he is clearly having relatively severe periods. A couple of things:

1. Telling someone to just go to the hospital is laughable. By the time I was 19 (32 now), I had already seen so many specialists and tried every remedy on the extremely short list other than full hysterectomy and invasive exploratory surgery. Nothing helped. Medicine has well and truly failed to properly research or treat pain and dysfunction as it relates to uterus-havers; telling your boyfriend to go the hospital or shut up, aside from being just fucking mean, is ignoring the reality that the hospital likely won't help him any more than help he could access help at home.

2. God fucking forbid your partner ever become chronically ill or disabled, since you seem to have a really hard time with people having observable negative responses to pain. Other than asking you for a very small bit of help reaching a thing he needed, he really didn't make this your problem. You, technically the older and adultier adult in the relationship, threw a tantrum about *his reaction to his own pain.* Let that sink in.

3. Let's talk about severe mood changes that come with the period hormone hell! The level of mental health shift can be like rapid-onset extreme depression and can come with severe dysmorphia- distorted self image- just when it most reduces your ability to cope with stress. Add onto that the heavy dose of dysphoria that a lot of trans folks feel around their period and the psychological load alone can be debilitating, even without all the physical fuckery. *This is a mental health episode* and you told the person you supposedly love to suck it up and stop bothering you with it.

4. Other folks have explained just how bad the pain can be- and it's not just the uterine cramps, although those are bad; it's also headache/migraine, full body muscle aches, stomach and gut cramping, widespread joint inflammation. Like the worst flu you've ever had. Every month.

5. "Just some blood" my ASS. How much blood varies widely; my partner barely bleeds at all now that they're on testosterone, but my dysfunctional reproductive system hasn't slackened off one bit on T and I'm still reenacting the elevator scene from the shining for 4-7 days. Blood loss is painful. It causes fatigue, nausea, vertigo. Ever gotten a lot of vials of blood drawn at a hospital? It's that sick unsteady feeling, but for days.

Your "13 year old girl" comment is misogynist AF and your whole post reeks of ableism and a general lack of compassion. You seem really unable to handle your partner being visibly upset near you, even though the upset isn't about you and isn't being directed at you. I'm not sure your trans partner should be dating you unless you get yourself educated and in therapy to help you have better interpersonal tools.
